summary: Updates requirements for supporting TCP as a transport for DNS, so implementations are expected to support it. It is a Proposed Standard and was replaced by RFC 7766.

eli5.summary: DNS usually uses small quick messages, but sometimes the answer is big, so computers must also be able to use the other, slower way. It was replaced by RFC 7766.

questions: why is tcp required for dns
subtitle: Why DNS implementations must support TCP in addition to UDP.

tldr.problem: DNS mostly uses UDP, a fast but size-limited protocol. When responses are too large to fit in one UDP packet, DNS needs an alternative.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC makes TCP support mandatory for all DNS implementations, not optional, so large responses can be delivered reliably when UDP alone is insufficient.
tldr.outcome: DNS now works reliably even when DNSSEC and other extensions make responses bigger than the original 512-byte limit. It was later updated by RFC 7766.

today: RFC 5966 established TCP as a mandatory part of DNS implementations in August 2010. It was later updated by RFC 7766 with additional clarifications.

sections.title: Why TCP Matters for DNS
sections.content:
The DNS protocol works primarily over UDP, a connectionless protocol that sends one message at a time with a maximum size limit. The original DNS specification from 1987 imposed a 512-byte limit on UDP responses. Zone transfers—the process of copying all records from one DNS server to another—have always required TCP because they often exceed this limit.

DNS specifies that when a response would exceed 512 bytes, the server should truncate it and set the TC (truncation) flag in the response header. The client then knows to retry the same query over TCP, which has no size limit. However, treating TCP as optional has caused interoperability problems. This RFC elevates TCP from an optional feature to a mandatory requirement for all DNS implementations.
sections.eli5: DNS is like sending a postcard: fast but small. A bigger answer needs a letter (TCP), which takes longer but has no size limit. Old DNS said postcard-first was OK, but now computers must know how to send letters too.

sections.title: The Size Problem and Modern DNS
sections.content:
When DNS Security (DNSSEC) was deployed in real systems, it made responses much larger. For example, an NXDOMAIN response (negative answer indicating a name does not exist) from a DNSSEC-signed zone using NSEC3 (Next Secured record hashing) is almost always larger than 512 bytes.

The DNS protocol supports EDNS0 (Extension Mechanisms for DNS), which allows clients to advertise that they can accept larger UDP responses. However, UDP packets larger than the path MTU (the maximum packet size networks can carry) must be fragmented into smaller pieces. Fragmented DNS packets are unreliable in practice: many firewalls block them, some network devices refuse to handle DNS packets with EDNS0 options, and reassembly often fails.

The core Internet MTU is typically around 1500 bytes, and even that is routinely exceeded by DNSSEC responses. TCP, which breaks data into smaller pieces automatically, is the only reliable way to handle large responses.
sections.eli5: Modern DNS with security signatures makes answers huge. Splitting big UDP messages breaks them. The future needs TCP, which automatically chops things into pieces that always arrive.

sections.title: TCP Support is Now Mandatory
sections.content:
All general-purpose DNS implementations MUST support both UDP and TCP transport. Specifically:

  • Authoritative servers (the servers that hold the official records) MUST support TCP so they can send responses of any size without truncation.
  • Recursive servers (which look up names on behalf of clients) MUST support TCP so they can relay large responses from other servers to their own clients.
  • Stub resolvers (the DNS client library on an operating system) MUST support TCP so they do not limit their ability to work with upstream servers.

The only exception is stub resolvers designed for restricted environments where responses are guaranteed never to be truncated.

The original RFC 1123 required that DNS resolvers "SHOULD" send a UDP query first before trying TCP. This RFC relaxes that requirement: resolvers SHOULD send UDP first, but MAY skip directly to TCP if they have good reason to expect truncation or if they already have an open TCP connection to the server.
sections.eli5: Every DNS program must know how to use TCP now. Try UDP first (it is faster), but switch to TCP if needed. Old advice only said "should," but now it is the rule.

sections.title: Managing Persistent TCP Connections
sections.content:
The original DNS specification suggested that servers could keep TCP connections open for about two minutes of idle time to allow zone transfer sequences to occur on a single connection. Modern protocols like HTTP have shown that long timeouts cause resource exhaustion and denial-of-service vulnerabilities.

The RFC recommends that the default idle timeout should be on the order of seconds, not minutes, though implementations may vary this dynamically based on load. Clients MUST minimize the number of concurrent TCP connections to any server to avoid overwhelming it. Servers MAY limit the number of concurrent connections from any client.
sections.eli5: Keep TCP connections for seconds, not minutes, so the server does not run out of space. Clients should not open tons of connections at once.

sections.title: Response Reordering and Out-of-Order Replies
sections.content: DNS allows queries and responses to arrive in any order, whether over UDP or TCP. Clients sending multiple queries at once cannot assume the replies arrive in the same order the queries were sent. Client software MUST be prepared to match responses to their corresponding requests by message ID, regardless of order.
sections.eli5: When you send several questions, the answers might come back scrambled. Always check which question each answer belongs to, not just the order they arrive.

sections.title: DoS Risks and Mitigation
sections.content:
Some DNS operators worried that TCP support would increase denial-of-service (DoS) attack risk. While TCP connections do have higher attack exposure than stateless UDP, network-level DoS defenses have improved substantially since DNS was designed. Most DNS servers today, including all root servers and most top-level domain (TLD) servers, support TCP and no evidence suggests that TCP-based attacks are widespread.

Operators of recursive servers should accept connections only from expected clients, not from unknown sources, to prevent both UDP reflector attacks and TCP connection exhaustion attacks.
sections.eli5: Attackers could create more problems with TCP. But the Internet's defenses are much better now, and almost every major DNS server already uses TCP safely.
